How Sportsbook Geolocation Actually Works

Published September 22, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Try opening a legal sportsbook app while standing a few feet on the wrong side of a state line, or from a hotel room with a spotty Wi-Fi router, and you'll run into one of the more mysterious parts of regulated betting: the app simply refuses to let you place a bet, sometimes with no clear explanation. That refusal isn't a glitch — it's geolocation working exactly as designed, and understanding how it actually determines your location explains a surprising number of "why won't this let me bet" moments that have nothing to do with your account.

In this guide

  1. Why geolocation exists in the first place
  2. The signals a sportsbook actually checks
  3. How the pieces get combined into one decision
  4. Where it reliably breaks down
  5. What operators do about VPNs and spoofing

Why geolocation exists in the first place

Legal sports betting in the United States is regulated state by state, and in nearly every state that has legalized it, the law requires that a bet be placed by someone physically located within that state's borders at the moment they place it — regardless of where they live, where their account is registered, or where they're a resident. That's a meaningfully different rule than the age or identity checks a sportsbook runs once at signup. Geolocation isn't a one-time gate; it's a check that has to run continuously, because a bettor's physical location can change from one bet to the next, or even mid-session if they're moving around near a border.

Regulators require operators to demonstrate this compliance to a fairly exacting standard, which is why geolocation isn't handled by a simple "what state did you select" dropdown. It's built on third-party geolocation vendors — GeoComply is the dominant one in the US regulated betting market — whose entire business is verifying real-world location to a standard that satisfies state gaming commissions, not just guessing based on convenience.

The signals a sportsbook actually checks

No single data point is trusted on its own, because each one has known weaknesses. Instead, geolocation software blends several signals and looks for agreement between them:

  • GPS. On a phone, this is usually the most precise signal available, often accurate to within a few meters outdoors. It's also the least reliable indoors or in dense urban areas, where satellite signal gets blocked or bounced off buildings.
  • Wi-Fi access point triangulation. Your device can see the signal strength of nearby Wi-Fi networks, and geolocation vendors maintain enormous databases mapping known router locations. Cross-referencing which networks you can "see," and how strong each one is, narrows your position even when GPS is weak — this is often what's doing the real work indoors.
  • Cell tower triangulation. Similar idea, using the cell towers your phone connects to and their known fixed locations, which helps fill gaps where GPS and Wi-Fi data are both thin.
  • IP address geolocation. Your internet connection's IP address maps to a general geographic region through public and licensed databases. This signal is coarse — sometimes accurate only to a metro area — and is treated as a supporting check rather than the primary one, partly because IP location is also the easiest signal to disguise with a VPN.
  • Device and network fingerprinting. Operators also look at signals like time zone settings, SIM card registration data, and known patterns associated with location-spoofing tools, mainly as a fraud-detection layer rather than a positioning method.

How the pieces get combined into one decision

The geolocation vendor's software runs on your device (usually through an SDK embedded in the sportsbook's app, or a browser plugin for desktop play) and packages up all the available signals, then sends that bundle to a verification service that cross-references it against known state boundaries — down to the specific address level in places where a state line runs through the middle of a building or a parking lot, which does happen at a handful of real-world locations near borders.

SignalTypical accuracyMain weakness
GPS~3–15 meters outdoorsDegrades badly indoors or in "urban canyon" areas with tall buildings
Wi-Fi triangulation~10–40 metersDepends on a populated database of nearby router locations
Cell tower triangulation~100 meters to a few kmCoarser in rural areas with fewer towers
IP addressCity to metro-area levelEasily masked by a VPN or proxy

The verification decision that comes back isn't binary "yes/no" from a single source — it's a confidence score built from how well the available signals agree with each other and how close the calculated position is to a legal boundary. A location comfortably inside a legal state with GPS, Wi-Fi, and cell data all pointing the same direction clears near-instantly. A location close to a border, or one where signals disagree with each other, is where things slow down or fail.

Where it reliably breaks down

A handful of situations account for most of the "why can't I bet right now" frustration bettors run into, even when nothing is actually wrong with their account:

The pattern to recognize: if a bet gets blocked and the app gives you a vague locate-failure message rather than an outright "you're not in a legal state" message, the likeliest explanation is a weak or conflicting signal environment, not an actual border violation.
  • Border towns and highway overlaps. Someone a mile from a state line, especially in a metro area that straddles two states (Kansas City, the DC area, parts of the Illinois–Indiana line), can get a Wi-Fi or cell signal reading that pulls their calculated position toward the wrong side, even while GPS shows them correctly.
  • Large buildings and basements. Casinos, stadiums, and big-box retail buildings can badly distort GPS, and if the building happens to sit near a legal boundary, that distortion matters a lot more.
  • Corporate VPNs and some routers. A workplace VPN that routes traffic through an out-of-state or out-of-country server can make the IP signal disagree sharply with GPS, triggering a fraud-style block even for someone who is legitimately in-state.
  • Airplane mode with Wi-Fi only. Disabling cellular service removes an entire category of corroborating signal, leaving the app to lean harder on Wi-Fi and GPS alone.
  • New or unmapped Wi-Fi networks. A newly installed router that isn't yet in the triangulation database contributes nothing useful, which matters more in areas with sparse Wi-Fi coverage to begin with.

What operators do about VPNs and spoofing

Because IP-based location is comparatively easy to fake with a VPN, and because a small number of people have tried using VPNs or GPS-spoofing apps to bet from states where online betting isn't legal, geolocation vendors build specific detection for exactly that. This includes maintaining databases of known VPN and proxy server IP ranges, checking for mismatches between a device's claimed GPS position and its network-inferred position, and flagging known jailbroken or spoofing-capable devices. Getting caught attempting this isn't a soft warning in most states — sportsbooks are contractually and legally obligated to block and often permanently ban accounts that attempt to circumvent geolocation, and a compliance failure exposes the operator itself to real regulatory risk, which is why the detection tends to be aggressive rather than lenient.

This is also why "just use a VPN" is bad advice you'll sometimes see repeated online — it's a Terms of Service violation nearly everywhere, it risks your funds and account standing, and in states where online sports betting isn't legal at all, attempting to access it through location spoofing can carry its own legal exposure separate from anything the sportsbook does.

What to do when you get blocked incorrectly

If you're legitimately in a legal state and getting blocked anyway, a few practical steps resolve most cases:

  1. Turn on both Wi-Fi and cellular data rather than relying on just one — more corroborating signals means a faster, more confident location fix.
  2. Disable any VPN, including one your employer may have auto-connected in the background.
  3. Move away from concrete-and-steel interiors (parking garages, basements, large box stores) toward a window or outdoors if you're getting repeated locate failures.
  4. If you're near a state line, expect more friction there generally — this isn't specific to any one operator, and it usually resolves by moving a reasonable distance further from the border.
  5. Check the app's support page for a geolocation troubleshooting tool; most major sportsbooks have a built-in diagnostic that shows which signal is failing, which is more useful than guessing.

For more on how state-level legality shapes what you can actually do on a given app, see our responsible gambling resources, or browse our sports betting guides for other basics that affect account setup and access.

Frequently asked questions

Does a sportsbook track my location when I'm not betting?

Generally, no — geolocation checks run when you attempt to place a bet or, on some apps, periodically while the betting app is actively open, not as continuous background tracking. Regulators require the check to be tied to active wagering, not general surveillance.

Can a sportsbook geolocate me if my phone's location services are off?

It can still attempt a location fix using Wi-Fi and cell signals, but the result will generally be far less precise, and most apps will simply refuse to let you bet until GPS or equivalent precise location access is granted.

Is geolocation the same thing as identity verification (KYC)?

No, they're separate systems solving separate problems. KYC confirms who you are and that you're of legal age, typically once at signup and occasionally again later. Geolocation confirms where your device physically is, and it runs every time you try to bet.

Why did my bet get blocked even though the app showed my correct state?

The state shown in the app's interface (often based on your account's registered address or a quick IP check) is different from the precise geolocation check run at the moment of betting. You can see a state name displayed correctly and still fail the stricter location check that actually gates whether the bet goes through.

Do airport hotels and casinos near state lines cause more geolocation problems?

Yes, disproportionately so. Large buildings degrade GPS, and if that building also happens to be close to a legal boundary, the combination of weak signal and proximity to a border is exactly the scenario where geolocation checks are most likely to stall or fail.
